To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) plants of Carduus may benefit from leaf cutting ants without being eaten; 2) the waste products produced by leaf cutting ants may reduce herbivore damage; and 3) the waste products may induce physical defense traits in plants.

1) leaf cutting ants may indirectly benefit the plants they do not eat, 2) this is the first case in which plants may plastically increase their physical defense against herbivores, 3) this plastic increase in physical defenses may prevent leaf cutting ants from harvesting the plant, 4) plants established in refuse may have fewer insect herbivores, and 5) the nutrient rich refuse may reduce the stage at leaf tenderness.
plants of Carduus increased their physical defenses and reduced insect damage when grown in the refuse dumps of Acromyrmec lobicornis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of ants on plant defense, and we have found a novel way by that plants may benefit from herbivore activity.
the role of plant defenses in mediating the interaction between plants and their consumers.
the role of plant defenses in the context of a mutualism between plants and ants and how this may influence herbivore pressure on plants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
plants may benefit from the presence of leaf cutting ants without being eaten.
leaf cutting ants indirectly increase the physical defenses of C. nutans by providing nutrients to plants.
plants of C. nutans grown in the refuse dumps of A. lobicornis have enhanced physical defenses and reduced insect herbivory.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
plants may benefit from herbivore consumers indirectly through waste products.
the leaf cutting ant indirectly improves anti herbivore defense of the plant by providing a nutrient rich refuse dump that reduces the stage at which the leaves are vulnerable to insect herbivory.
plants can respond to the presence of ants by increasing their physical defenses, which in turn reduces the probability that the plants will be harvested by the ants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
plants may benefit from the presence of herbivores via the waste they produce.
plant defenses may be induced by cues other than herbivory.
the effects of herbivores can be positive for plants, but not through the direct consumption.
